1:
The opening notice is read against its parallel in Kings, and the age is unsettled. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds the verse identical with that parallel, but records that the Greek, Syriac and Arabic all read twenty-five rather than twenty, and that some manuscripts and the Syriac add the words his God to the divine name as Kings does. John Gill (reformed) says only that these verses are much the same as the parallel, with one difference of wording there. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) does not resolve the figure either, referring the difficulties of the chronology to his note on the other passage. Ellicott adds what none of the others has, that the Assyrian monuments call this king Yahuhazi, that is Jehoahaz, of which Ahaz may be a familiar abridgement, on the pattern by which Jonathan becomes Nathan.

What walking in the ways of the kings of Israel meant is answered by Ellicott alone. The molten images were made for the Baals, that is for the different aspects of the Canaanite god, and the clause is the chronicler’s own addition explaining the one before it: the way of those kings was the state recognition of Baal worship side by side with that of Jehovah. He allows the alternative that this clause and the first of the next verse may simply have fallen out of the text of Kings, which is Thenius’s view of the passage. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep their comment for the war that follows, referring the course of it to their treatment of the parallel and observing only that the chronicler brings the two main battles prominently forward.

On the valley where the incense was burnt Ellicott traces a word into the New Testament. The incense went to Moloch, the god of Ammon, for whom Solomon had built a high place that was still standing; the valley lay west and south of the city and was the scene of the cruel rites in honour of that god, whom he quotes Milton calling a horrid king besmeared with blood. In later times the name of the valley, spelt as one word and with modified vowels, became the appellation of hell, the house of woe and pain; it is used so in the Targums and afterwards in the Talmud, and it reaches the New Testament in a Graecised form from which the Latin name of hell descends.

That Ahaz burnt his children in the plural is treated as a textual question and as a legend. Ellicott notes that Kings says rather that he made his own son pass through the fire, and that the chronicler has reached burning by transposing two Hebrew letters; the plural he takes for a generalised expression, as one might say that a man burnt his own offspring. Thenius accuses the chronicler of exaggerating, but Ellicott answers that this use of the plural is one of the marks of his style. Clarke sets beside the verse a remarkable addition in the Chaldee, which has the Word of the Lord snatch Hezekiah from among the children Ahaz burnt, because the three righteous men Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were to proceed from him and were themselves to be delivered from a burning furnace for the sake of the great and glorious Name. The passage then numbers five escapes from fire: Abram cast in by Nimrod for refusing the idols, Tamar in the house of judgment of Judah, Hezekiah thrown by his father into the valley on the altars of Tophet, the three men in the furnace of Nebuchadnezzar, and Joshua the son of Josedek, who escaped for his righteousness where two others cast in with him were consumed.
5:
That the text calls the Lord his God, of such a king, is answered by two. John Gill (reformed) gives three grounds: God was his of right, having dominion over him and deserving his worship; his by the national covenant with the people Ahaz was king of; and his by Ahaz’s own hypocritical profession, while he forsook the true worship. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts the same thing more sharply, that God was his God not by the special relation, which Ahaz had renounced, but by sovereign dominion — for God did not forfeit his right by Ahaz denying it.

Why this account differs from the one in Kings is Ellicott’s question, answered from the writer’s purpose. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) holds that the chronicler means not so much to describe a campaign as to select the events that most conspicuously illustrate God’s chastisement of an apostate king, so that the historical is subordinated to the didactic: not history for its own sake, but history teaching by example. He adds that this does not make the events doubtful, Thenius having characterised the whole section as thoroughly historical. So instead of the joint attempt on Jerusalem and the seizure of the southern port, the chronicler prefers two severe defeats in the open field before the retreat behind the walls; after which the confederates converged on the capital, the panic at their coming being finely depicted by Isaiah, and their attempt proving ineffectual as that prophet had foretold.

The casualty figures divide the voices three ways, and the disagreement is substantive. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) doubts them outright: very probably there is a mistake, since it is hardly possible that a hundred and twenty thousand men were slain in one day — and yet, he concedes, all the versions and manuscripts agree in it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) defend the figures against named critics who declared them the exaggerations of a wonder-loving chronicler; in this, they say, the critics are mistaken, for Isaiah shows the allied kings purposed to annihilate Judah outright, and the Ephraimites always acted with extreme cruelty in war. Ellicott treats both totals as round numbers, observes that the figure would mean about a third of the Jewish host fell in the battle and pursuit, and then produces the corroboration no one else has: Sennacherib boasts of taking forty-six strong cities of Judah and carrying off two hundred thousand one hundred and fifty captives, so that the figure here is confirmed from a foreign and wholly unrelated source. Both he and Keil and Delitzsch note that brethren is used with emphasis, marking the cruelty of carrying off the defenceless women and children of one’s own kin; Gill accounts for the ease of it, that after such a slaughter of the men the rest were intimidated.

The three men killed beside the king are identified alike by two, and Gill adds a link back. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that the king’s son cannot be a son of Ahaz, who so early could not have had a son old enough to bear arms, but a prince of the royal house, a cousin or an uncle; that the governor of the house was a palace official rather than a temple one; and that the third was the second from the king, his first minister. Ellicott says why the three are named at all: their intimate connection with Ahaz is the point, since the blow that struck them struck the king whose punishment is described. He glosses in one day as one great engagement, the word day bearing among Hebrews and Arabs the force of a day of battle. Gill, remembering the third verse, observes that this king’s son must then have escaped being burnt in the valley of Hinnom, or was only made to pass through the fire there.
9:
Who this prophet was draws two observations about his famous contemporary, pointing opposite ways. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the whole section is peculiar to the chronicler, who told it his own way, so that the words of the prophet and the chiefs may be mainly his, though there is no ground for doubting its general truth; of Oded nothing further is known, and he was a prophet of Jehovah, not of the Baals. What Ellicott finds remarkable is a silence: neither here nor in the parallel is any mention of Hosea, who must have been active at this epoch in the northern kingdom. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reach for Hosea to the contrary purpose, as proof that a true prophet could be found in Samaria at all — not of the Jahve there worshipped in the calf images but of the true God, like Hosea, who laboured in the ten tribes at that time — and compare his going to meet the army with Azariah meeting Asa. John Gill (reformed) says only that he is not the Oded of Asa’s day.

The rebuke is analysed closely by the two grammarians. Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet quicken the conscience first and only then demand: the butchery was already a sin crying to heaven, and carrying off the women and children filled up its measure, so that the question whether there are not sins with them, even with them, asserts in a lively way what is not in doubt. Ellicott puts it more bluntly: the victory was owed to the punitive wrath of Jehovah, not to their own valour or intrinsic superiority, which they ought to have considered and shown compassion to the victims of divine displeasure, whereas they gave full rein to the savage dictates of furious hatred. He reads the question either as whether they are wholly guiltless or whether they are the only guiltless people, the reference perhaps being to the calves of Bethel and Dan; and he notes that the law forbids the permanent enslaving of Israelites by Israelites.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) declines to comment and then gives the chapter’s strongest verdict. To this beautiful speech, he says, nothing can be added by the best comment: it is simple, humane, pious and overwhelmingly convincing, and no wonder it produced the effect recorded. That the Ephraimite chiefs had much humanity the fifteenth verse proves, for they did not barely dismiss these unfortunate captives but took the very spoil their army had brought away, and clothed, fed, shod and anointed them, set the feeblest upon asses and escorted them safely to Jericho. We can scarcely find a parallel to it, he concludes, in the universal history of the wars savage man has carried on against his fellows from the foundation of the world.

Ellicott asks why the chronicler lingers on the kindness, and answers three ways. The writer dwells with manifest pleasure on the mercy of these repentant foes, and may have meant a lesson for the Samaritans of his own age, whose hostility so damaged the restored exiles and who by rabbinic tradition tried to prejudice Alexander the Great against Jerusalem. Some have supposed, he adds, that our Lord had this passage in mind in the parable of the good Samaritan, the coincidences being at any rate curious. And he defends the episode by symmetry: an Ephraimite prophet interposing between Ephraimites and their Judaean captives is precisely parallel to the Judaean prophet Shemaiah interposing between his people and the ten tribes, so that granting the truth of the one leaves no ground for suspecting the other. Keil and Delitzsch call the description picturesque; and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) finds in the surrender a more truly heroic bravery than the taking, since it is true honour to yield to reason and religion even in spite of interest.
16:
Why the text says kings of Assyria, in the plural, is answered four ways. John Gill (reformed) takes it literally of Tiglath-pileser and his son, noting that the Greek, Latin, Syriac and Targum read the singular. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) treats the singular as the true text, the versions and the parallel place having it. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps the plural but lowers it to princes, called kings in a looser sense. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) calls it a generalised expression of the kind the chronicler uses elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) alone make it carry a charge: the plural is rhetorical, since the chronicler himself shows later that only one king was approached, and by it the thought is expressed that Ahaz, instead of seeking the help of his own God which the prophet had promised, turned to the kings of a world-power hostile to the kingdom of God, from whom he could get no real help.

The two invasions that followed are read as opportunism. Keil and Delitzsch have the Edomites, subdued lately by Amaziah and Uzziah and freed by Rezin, seize the moment for vengeance; and the Philistines, whom Uzziah had subdued, use the pressure of Syrians and Ephraimites not merely to shake off their yoke but to enlarge their territory by capturing towns. Ellicott sets out the ground taken, the lowland between the hill-country and the sea and the southland of Judah, and reads the closing clause strictly: they did not raid but permanently occupied it. Gill has them fall first on the cities nearest them and press as far as the south, in revenge for what Uzziah had done.

That Ahaz is called king of Israel divides them, and they reject one another explicitly. Gill explains it three ways: because he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, because he ruled two of the tribes, and because of right he was king over all Israel as David and Solomon had been — noting that the Greek, Latin and Syriac read Judah, as does the Targum. Keil and Delitzsch deny the first of those reasons and make the title ironical, his government having been the bitterest satire upon the name of a king of Israel, that is of the people of God. Ellicott rejects the irony most commentators see and holds that the southern kingdom simply was Israel in the chronicler’s idea, however much more important the northern was politically — as the cedar of Lebanon beside the blackthorn beside it — On making Judah naked, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree the verb means Ahaz behaved loosely in Judah rather than that he made Judah loose, the construction forbidding the latter; Gill and Wesley take the nakedness as stripping — of treasure, of frontier towns, and above all of religion and the divine protection, which Wesley calls their only firm security.

On the help that was no help, Wesley supplies the argument others only assert. Ellicott describes what the Assyrian wanted: glad of a pretext for interference in the west, the usurper was bent on extending his empire, and once Syria and Israel lay at his feet he required an unequivocal acknowledgement of vassalage, distressing Ahaz by reducing the kingdom to a dependency and stripping the treasure sent as the price of that ruinous help; he quotes a modern historian that the principle of that monarchy was plunder and its kings had no regard to their vassals. Clarke says simply that the Assyrian did him no ultimate service. Wesley explains why not, and it is the sharpest thing here: the expression is most emphatical, for though Tiglath weakened the Syrian, who, troublesome neighbour though he was, had served Judah as a kind of bulwark, his removal only smoothed the way for a far more dangerous enemy — as appeared in the very next reign.
22:
That the text says the gods of Damascus smote him is felt as a scandal, and four voices meet it four ways. John Gill (reformed) first takes it of Ahaz’s folly, imagining they might do him no more hurt, as it is said of the Indians that they worship the devil so that he may not hurt them — monstrous stupidity in a king of Judah — then proposes a construction saving the writer: the meaning may rather be the gods of those who smote him, the men of Damascus, for the Spirit of God would never ascribe the smiting to idols, however Ahaz might. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) quotes a commentator surprised on the same ground, that Scripture everywhere represents heathen idols as nothing and vanity, incapable of good or hurt, so that an inspired author cannot have written this; the difficulty is avoided by following the older Hebrew copies behind the Greek, which make the words Ahaz’s own — I will seek to the gods of Damascus which have smitten me — a turn the Syriac and Arabic share.

Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) puts the question others avoid: did the chronicler himself believe the gods of Aram had any real existence? That the Israelites of Ahaz’s day commonly believed it he thinks certain; and while the latter half of Isaiah asserts the nothingness of false gods, another opinion also ran, which Paul repeats and Milton adopted, that what the heathen sacrifice they sacrifice to demons. He also reads the closing clause as pointed: those very gods were to him a stumbling, and to all Israel. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) fight instead over a participle, insisting against Bertheau that it must not be rendered as a pluperfect: Ahaz sought the Syrian gods’ help not after the Syrians had defeated him but while they were defeating him, during the war and not after it —.

On the spoiling of the temple the accounts complement each other. Keil and Delitzsch say he was not content with strange gods but laid hands on the vessels and suppressed the worship, cautioning that the gathering and the word all are rhetorical; the cutting, by the parallel account, meant mutilating the wrought vessels of the court and taking the brazen sea down from its oxen onto a stone pavement. Ellicott glosses the verb as trimming off their metal ornaments, notes the shutting of the doors is absent from Kings, insists it was the sanctuary doors and not the great court’s, so that all rites confined to the Holy Place were suspended, and suggests the sacrilege was committed in collecting anything of value for the rapacious Assyrian. Clarke notes the doors stayed shut until the next reign.

The judgment on the man, and the burial, close the chapter. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) is the most violent: that monster and reproach of mankind, that unteachable and incorrigible prince, whom even grievous afflictions made worse where they commonly make men better, and whose name deserves to be remembered and detested for ever. Ellicott makes the point from the grammar, the subject being emphatically repeated so that it reads he, king Ahaz, the notorious apostate, who having been sorely chastised sinned yet more. On the burial Keil and Delitzsch find a deliberate choice of words: he was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, but not in the graves of the kings, the phrasing seeming selected to intimate that one who had not walked like his ancestor David was not laid beside him. Ellicott notes the clause is wanting in Kings and answers Thenius, who supposed it founded on mistake or on zeal for the Law, with the obvious alternative — why not upon a written authority? Clarke thinks the matter of little importance, taking it as this writer’s common habit of putting Israel for Judah, considering them one people from one stock.
